ta-l1d40q3-d1e100.summary: The third question of Distinction 40 asks about the certainty of predestination, with a first argument that it is not certain. Rev. 3:11 says 'hold what you have, lest another take your crown'. This cannot mean the crown of present justice, since grace is destroyed by sin and not transferred, so it means the crown of glory, which belongs to someone in this life only as predestined to him, so one can receive what was predestined to another.

ta-l1d40q3-d1e107.summary: Second argument. Gregory says when some fall, others succeed to their places, and a place of glory is theirs only as predestined to them.
claims: Others succeed to the places of the fallen.

ta-l1d40q3-d1e110.summary: Third argument. Ps. 68:29 says 'let them be blotted out of the book of the living', and what is not written cannot be blotted out, and predestination is the book of life.
claims: Names can be blotted out of the book of life.

ta-l1d40q3-d1e116.summary: Fourth argument. There is no certainty of what is determined neither in itself nor in its causes, and movements of free choice, a cause open to either, are not determined before they occur, and predestination's effect is fulfilled through meritorious acts of free choice.

ta-l1d40q3-d1e119.summary: Fifth argument. Certain knowledge posited necessarily implies the known. Predestination, being eternal, can be posited at any time, so someone can be posited predestined before he is saved, and 'he will be saved' concluded as true; but if a future contingent were true it would happen necessarily (the Philosopher), so he would necessarily be saved, destroying free choice, which is impossible, and only the impossible yields the impossible.
claims: Certain predestination would make salvation necessary.

ta-l1d40q3-d1e122.summary: Sed contra. Predestination includes foreknowledge, and God has certain knowledge of all he knows (cross-reference to Dist. 36).

ta-l1d40q3-d1e125.summary: Thomas's determination. Some said God knows future contingents only as they are, knowing them to be contingent as necessaries to be necessary, but Boethius refutes this, since then God would know no more of future salvation than man, who also knows it to be contingent. Others said the number of the saved is certain to God as a number by which we count (a hundred or a thousand will be saved) but not materially, as to supposits, since these people can be saved or not; but this attributes imperfect, merely universal knowledge to God, and if he knows these people will be saved it must be certain, since his knowledge can no more be uncertain than false. So the number of the predestined, formally and materially, is certain to God and uncertain to us. This certainty imposes no necessity on those to be saved. Predestination includes foreknowledge and providence of salvation; providence, though of all things, does not make all happen necessarily, but according to the condition of proximate causes, whose natures and order providence and predestination preserve. Foreknowledge imposes no necessity either as cause, since it is first cause, whose condition the effect does not have but that of the proximate cause, or by its adequation to the known, required for truth and certainty, since this adequation is of God's knowledge to the thing not as in its causes, where it is only a possible future, but as having determinate being, as present, not future (Dist. 38).
claims: The number of the predestined is certain to God formally and materially, uncertain to us.
This certainty imposes no necessity, since effects follow proximate causes and God knows things as present.

ta-l1d40q3-d1e129.summary: Reply to the first argument. It can be expounded either way. Of the crown of present justice: another takes his crown when his works done in charity, profiting himself and others since the spirit of charity makes the saints' merits common, cease to profit him for eternal life when he sins, while their fruit remains in those who persevere, not that numerically the same grace passes to another. Of the crown of future glory: the saints in heaven rejoice in all the merits of the saints on earth, so when someone with many prior merits sins, the joy of those merits remains eternally in the blessed, which he lost, not that the glory predestined to one is given to another. The text is said not to exclude the certainty of predestination but to show the freedom of choice.
claims: Another 'takes one's crown' by sharing the fruit of merits one loses, not by receiving one's predestined glory.

ta-l1d40q3-d1e135.summary: Reply to the second argument. Gregory speaks not of the place predestined for the saints but of the place they hold in the Church by present justice, since the Church is never without people in grace, so when some sin, God calls others to grace.
claims: Gregory means places in the Church, not in glory.

ta-l1d40q3-d1e138.summary: Reply to the third argument. Predestination is the book of life as something is written in it as to future glory as well as present justice, and so no one can be blotted out; what is written there as to present justice only is said to be blotted out, not by change in the book, but in the person written there, who changes from present justice, so that his life is represented not as present but as past.
claims: Blotting out concerns those written only as to present justice, and the change is in them.

ta-l1d40q3-d1e141.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. A future contingent, like a movement of free choice, though not determined in its cause, is determined in its being as actual and so falls under the certainty of foreknowledge (Dist. 38).
claims: Free acts are determined as actual and so certainly foreknown.

ta-l1d40q3-d1e144.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. What is measured by eternity is simultaneous with all time without being measured by any time, so the act of divine foreknowledge cannot be posited as now, measured by present time, relating to its object as present to future; it relates to every time and every object as present to present. So 'God foreknows this' means it is future not relative to divine knowledge but to the time in which it is said, and such verbs and participles said of God must be freed from temporal determination to co-signify the now of eternity, not of time, or error inevitably follows.
claims: Divine foreknowledge relates to all times as present; temporal words about God must signify the eternal now.

ta-l1d40q3.summary: Quaestio 3 of Book I, Distinction 40 treats the certainty of predestination. Against views that God knows the saved only as contingent or only by number, Thomas holds that the number of the predestined is certain to God, formally and materially, though uncertain to us. This imposes no necessity, since effects follow proximate causes and God's eternal knowledge regards things as present. Texts about losing one's crown, others succeeding to places, and being blotted out of the book of life concern shared merits, places in the Church, and those written only as to present justice. Temporal language about God must be read as the eternal now.
claims: The number of the predestined is certain to God without imposing necessity.
God's foreknowledge regards all times as present.
